In the spring of 2003, Barbra Streisand filed a $50 million lawsuit in Los Angeles Superior Court to force the removal of a single aerial photograph showing her cliff-top Malibu residence. The image had been taken as one data point among 12,000 others in a public project mapping California’s eroding coastline and had been downloaded only six times before the legal papers arrived. ### Segment 2 — The Good Intention
Barbra Streisand acted out of a desire shared by many public figures of her era: to shield her private life from constant scrutiny. By the early 2000s, high-resolution digital photography and the growing reach of the internet had made it easier than ever for images of celebrities’ homes to circulate without consent, raising legitimate worries about security and personal boundaries. ### Segment 4 — The Unintended Consequences
Once the lawsuit became public knowledge, the opposite of containment occurred. Tech journalist Mike Masnick later coined the term “Streisand Effect” in 2005 to describe how attempts to suppress information online reliably increase its visibility. ### Segment 5 — The Aftermath
The California court’s ruling left the image online and established no new precedent restricting public coastal photography. Streisand moved on to other projects, but the episode became a recurring reference point in discussions of digital privacy and censorship. In July 1960, Egyptian engineers began diverting the Nile at Aswan to lay the foundation of a dam that would finally tame the river’s annual flood. The structure, completed a decade later, delivered reliable electricity and ended the centuries-old cycle of destructive high water. After the United States and Britain withdrew financing offers in 1956, Nasser turned to the Soviet Union, which supplied technical expertise and roughly one-third of the project’s cost. ### Segment 5 — The Aftermath
By 2017 Rosenstein had left Facebook and begun limiting his own use of social media, telling interviewers he kept his phone in grayscale and avoided the platforms he had helped shape. sections.lesson:
### Segment 6 — The Lesson
Simple, low-friction signals tend to become the dominant currency in any system that measures them, because they are cheap to produce and easy to compare. When those signals are attached to human identity rather than to the content itself, they reshape behavior at scale. Designers and policymakers therefore face a recurring choice: either accept that the metric will drive the activity, or deliberately limit how visible and consequential the metric is allowed to become.
